findings.passage: Yet in a decade of interviews about the films that went wrong, she has never described a set as a place where she was misled or left unprotected. Her complaint, every time, is the one she gave at Cannes: the movie that reached the screen was not the movie she signed up to make.
findings.problem: The hinge of the profile is written as biography ("never," "every time," and later "she separates them herself") when it is the author's weighing of a record the draft itself admits is incomplete ("There are things that I still cannot say"). The record is also less clean than the absolute allows. In the same Bustle answer the draft quotes for "It's contrived," she said of the author's involvement, "It's also about control and feeling powerful, and that's not what art is"; that is a grievance about an authority's power, and the draft omits it. Her 2026 line about sets where people were "not taken care of or not seen on set" and the July 2025 Variety line in the evidence record, "I can't waste time on toxic sets anymore," both describe sets as places where people go unprotected. James's 2015 "I had to fight for a lot of things really hard" was said before the film opened, about readers, and cannot characterize the fight as "rather than a betrayal." The FAQ repeats the absolute ("never that she was misled or left unprotected"). The reader is told what her grievances are about as a fact about her rather than as this profile's reading.
findings.acceptance_test: Both sentences, the "she separates them herself" sentence and the Type 6 FAQ are scoped to the reviewed record and marked as the profile's reading (for example, "in the interviews opened for this profile, the complaint she states is..."); the "control and feeling powerful" line is quoted beside "It's contrived" with a sentence on what it does to the test; the James 2015 quote is not used to characterize the shape of the fight; the C95 review trigger stays.

findings.passage: Accepting a depression-advocacy award in November 2023, she described a low day her partner caught before she did: "it turns out, I really was struggling. But that moment lifted me up and pulled me out of it."
findings.problem: This anecdote is counted in "The case for Type 6" as a remedy pattern (a trusted person notices and lifts her) three paragraphs before the article promises that her depression and therapy "are a medical matter and are not counted for any type." The speech was given at a depression-advocacy luncheon and describes a depressive low day. The evidence record's own alternative for C183 says the anecdote is about a medical condition and is not type evidence on its own. Weighing it for Six, or for Four's wish to be seen, treats a symptom as temperament and makes the article's stated rule untrue.
findings.acceptance_test: The anecdote is removed from the type argument, or kept only with an explicit sentence that it describes a depressive episode and is weighed for neither Six nor Four; after the edit the sentence "not counted for any type" is true of every passage in the article.

findings.passage: She prizes chosen family over "the people you're actually born to."
findings.problem: In the Bustle Q&A (reopened for this review) she was explaining the proverb while celebrating her big blended family, answering a question about Gwyneth Paltrow's post and her siblings: "I have four brothers and two sisters, and my two sisters are not blood-related to each other, but they are sisters and they call each other sisters." The chosen family she meant was her own non-blood siblings. Placed two sections after her parents' divorce and "well-publicized struggles with drugs and alcohol," the draft's sentence reads as a ranking of chosen people above her birth family, a claim about her family relationships she did not make.
findings.acceptance_test: The line is quoted in its blended-family context (siblings "not blood-related" who "call each other sisters"), or the sentence is cut; any Six loyalty point rests on that original context and does not imply distance from her parents.

findings.passage: In 2024: the author "was extremely precious about words, clothing, anything, everything," and there was "no room for being expressive or discovering what is present in that real moment that you're capturing. It's contrived." (Bustle)
findings.problem: This is the harshest characterization of E.L. James in the article, about a named person who has not responded, and it arrives with a bare "(Bustle)" tag. The disclosure that Johnson said she had "exaggerated in this interview" sits three sections earlier under the Type 6 case. In the same section, "she rewrote scenes the night before" drops her own qualifier, "with the old dialogue so I could add a line here and there," which shrinks what she described doing to James's material.
findings.acceptance_test: A short local reminder of the exaggeration caveat appears with the "extremely precious" line (or the caveat sentence moves to its first James-related use), and the rewriting claim carries her "add a line here and there" qualifier.

findings.passage: Even the confession is a bit, and it changes between tellings.
findings.problem: An inference about her intent stated as fact; the December 2021 telling could be an ordinary clarification. The same voice appears in "What she withheld was the fight." and in the closing "What she keeps losing, and keeps going back to build, is the connection inside it." The standard asks for local phrasing that separates observation from the profile's interpretation; the footer disclaimer does not license certainty here.
findings.acceptance_test: Each of the three sentences is marked as the profile's reading (for example, "reads as a bit," "what she appears to have withheld," "what she describes losing") or is tied to her own words that establish it.

findings.passage: told a Cannes audience in May 2025 what it had been like, more than once, to star in a film she did not recognize.
findings.problem: "A film she did not recognize" outruns her words, "That is not what I thought we were making," and the next sentence's "Her verdict on those nights" presents the two quoted fragments as adjacent when the evidence record (S53) states that adjacency between the Variety fragments is not asserted. A hook should not paraphrase her more sharply than she spoke.
findings.acceptance_test: The hook paraphrase stays within her quoted words (for example, seeing at a premiere a film that was not what she thought she had been making) and the adjacency implication is dropped unless the talk is opened and the sequence confirmed.

findings.passage: On regret: "It would've been like, 'Oh, this is psychotic.' But no, I don't regret it."
findings.problem: The quotation drops the conditional that gives "psychotic" its meaning: "If I had known at the time that's what it was going to be like, I don't think anyone would've done it." (Vanity Fair, reopened for this review.) Without it, "psychotic" floats as her description of the finished experience, and her stronger claim, that nobody would have signed on with foreknowledge, is lost.
findings.acceptance_test: The conditional clause is restored before "It would've been like," or the "psychotic" fragment is cut and only "But no, I don't regret it" is kept.

findings.passage: The author, E.L. James, whose real name is Erika Mitchell,
findings.problem: An unattributed legal-name claim about a third party. Vanity Fair, the source quoted in that paragraph, says only "E.L. James, who goes by Erika"; "Erika Mitchell" is The Hollywood Reporter's phrasing (her birth surname), and public records give her name as Erika Leonard. The evidence record attributes the name to THR; the article does not.
findings.acceptance_test: The clause uses Vanity Fair's "who goes by Erika" or attributes the name to The Hollywood Reporter; the profile does not assert a legal name as its own fact.

protected_passages.passage: In the same passage she added, "There are things that I still cannot say because I don't want to hurt anyone's career and I don't want to damage anybody's reputation, but both Jamie and I were treated really well."
protected_passages.reason: Keeps her own concessions beside her complaint; the fairness of the Fifty Shades material to James and Dornan depends on this line staying next to the dispute.

protected_passages.passage: Her depression, which she dates to "15 or 14," and the therapy she credits are a medical matter and are not counted for any type.
protected_passages.reason: The right principle for a subject who is a depression advocate; keep it and make the article honor it (see subject-02).

protected_passages.passage: A childhood like that can produce privacy, vigilance and a sense of not belonging in almost anyone, so it can't settle her type.
protected_passages.reason: Refuses childhood-wound causation in the paragraph that carries the most sensitive family material, all of it attributed to Vogue rather than to her.

protected_passages.passage: The limits are real. Nearly all of this is self-report in promotional settings, "authentic" and "different" are industry vocabulary, the other party to her central dispute has not answered, and "I don't want to hurt anyone's career" could be covering a trust grievance she has chosen not to voice. The Six reading is not refuted, only outweighed on content. Hence medium confidence.
protected_passages.reason: Honest inference limits that name the missing response and the incentive problem; this is where the profile stops speaking for her.

protected_passages.passage: She also warned that she had "exaggerated in this interview," so every Bustle line here carries that caveat.
protected_passages.reason: Discloses her own caveat on the source that supplies the sharpest lines about her and about James; keep, and extend locally per subject-04.

assessment: Fairness proxy read of the frozen draft against the evidence record, with Vanity Fair 2022 and Bustle 2024 reopened. The draft is careful where it most needs to be: family history and the tabloid-in-class anecdote are attributed to Vogue, not to her; the Fifty Shades account travels with her praise of James, her "treated really well" concession, James's own 2015 position and a dated note that no response has been found; the Ellen exchange is quoted only where the speaker is unambiguous; the depression principle is stated; the Bustle exaggeration caveat is disclosed; the limits paragraph names the missing response. The overclaims are of confidence, not harm. First, the discriminator is written as something she did ("never," "every time," "she separates them herself") rather than as the profile's reading, and the record contains lines that cut against the absolute ("control and feeling powerful," "toxic sets," "not taken care of ... on set"). Second, a depressive-episode anecdote from an advocacy speech is weighed as Type 6 evidence despite the article's own rule. Third, the chosen-family line is lifted out of a celebration of her blended family and reads as a judgment on her birth family. The remaining findings are local: a missing caveat beside the harshest James line, a regret quote cut from its conditional, intent statements in the author's voice, a hook paraphrase sharper than her words, and an unattributed legal name. Similarity: every tripped pair matches this subject's own prior draft from the 2026-10-07 run, which records continuity between runs, not formulaic writing; the highest cross-subject score (0.053, Jeremy Allen White) shares no phrases beyond ordinary "cannot settle" type vocabulary, so no reuse finding. Risks are carried unchanged from the evidence record (sensitive allegations and contested typing true), so the six-role jury already applies; no new risk is raised. This review does not speak for Dakota Johnson; it checks what the public record supports.
